notice: RN bank batch 28: Maternity III: postpartum and newborn care. Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026. See REVIEW-LOG.md.

questions.stem: Four hours after birth, the client's fundus is above the umbilicus and pushed to the right. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Help the client empty her bladder

rationale.correct: A displaced, high fundus suggests bladder distention; have the client void, then reassess.

perOption.a: A full bladder displaces the uterus and keeps it from contracting.
perOption.b: Emptying the bladder corrects the cause.
perOption.c: The likely cause is the bladder.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: One hour after birth, the client's fundus is soft and boggy at the umbilicus, and lochia is heavy. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Call the provider before doing anything
Place the client flat and wait

rationale.correct: Uterine atony is the most common cause of postpartum hemorrhage; massage first, then give uterotonics.

perOption.a: Massage stimulates the uterus to contract and reduces bleeding.
perOption.b: Massage comes first, then notify if bleeding continues.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A postpartum client with heavy bleeding has a blood pressure of 152/98 mm Hg. Which prescribed uterotonic should the nurse question?

rationale.correct: Methylergonovine: avoid with hypertension or preeclampsia. Carboprost: avoid with asthma.

perOption.a: Methylergonovine causes vasoconstriction and is contraindicated with hypertension.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: Which postpartum finding requires immediate follow-up?

options.text: Saturating a perineal pad in 15 minutes
Small clots, smaller than a quarter

rationale.correct: Report a pad saturated in 15 minutes, large clots, a boggy uterus or signs of shock.

perOption.a: This indicates hemorrhage.
perOption.b: Lochia rubra is expected for 1 to 3 days.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A postpartum client's fundus is firm and midline, but a steady trickle of bright red blood continues. What does the nurse suspect?

rationale.correct: Firm uterus with bleeding: suspect a laceration or hematoma and notify the provider.

perOption.a: Bleeding with a firm uterus suggests trauma, not atony.
perOption.b: With atony the uterus is boggy.
perOption.c: A continuous bright red trickle isn't normal.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: On postpartum day 3, a client has a temperature of 38.6 °C (101.5 °F), a tender uterus and foul-smelling lochia. What does the nurse suspect?

rationale.correct: Endometritis is more common after cesarean birth; it needs antibiotics.

perOption.a: Infection of the uterine lining causes fever, tenderness and foul lochia.
perOption.b: Fever and foul lochia aren't normal.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: On postpartum day 3, a client cries easily and feels overwhelmed but is caring for her baby. What is the best nursing response?

options.text: Explain that postpartum blues are common and short-lived, offer support and teach the signs of depression

rationale.correct: Postpartum blues: within 2 weeks, mild; depression: lasts longer and impairs function; psychosis: an emergency.

perOption.a: Baby blues affect most mothers and usually resolve within 2 weeks.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: One week after birth, a client says voices are telling her the baby is evil. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Make sure the infant is safe and the mother isn't left alone with the baby, and get emergency psychiatric evaluation
Reassure her that these are normal new-mother worries

rationale.correct: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency.

perOption.a: Postpartum psychosis puts both mother and baby at risk.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: Which observation shows that a newborn is latched on correctly?

options.text: The mouth is wide open, lips flanged outward and much of the areola is in the mouth
Only the nipple is in the baby's mouth
The cheeks pull in with each suck

rationale.correct: Good latch: wide mouth, flanged lips, audible swallowing, no pain after the first moments.

perOption.a: A deep latch allows effective feeding and prevents nipple pain.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A breastfeeding client on day 4 has swollen, hard, painful breasts. What should the nurse suggest?

options.text: Breastfeed often, apply warmth before feeding and cold packs after
Stop breastfeeding until the swelling goes down

rationale.correct: Engorgement: feed often, warm before, cold after, and express milk if needed.

perOption.a: Frequent emptying relieves engorgement; warmth helps let-down and cold reduces swelling.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A breastfeeding client has mastitis and is prescribed antibiotics. What should the nurse tell her?

options.text: "Keep breastfeeding or pumping from both breasts."
"Stop breastfeeding until the antibiotics are finished."

rationale.correct: Mastitis: keep emptying the breast, rest, fluids and antibiotics.

perOption.a: Emptying the breast helps clear the infection, and the milk is safe for the baby.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: At 1 minute, a newborn has a heart rate of 110/min, a weak, irregular cry, some flexion of the extremities, a grimace with suctioning, and a pink body with blue hands and feet. What is the Apgar score?

rationale.correct: Heart rate 110 (above 100) = 2. Respiratory effort weak and irregular = 1. Muscle tone some flexion = 1. Reflex irritability grimace = 1. Color acrocyanosis = 1. Total = 6.
references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: Immediately after a healthy term birth, what should the nurse do first?

options.text: Dry the newborn and place the baby skin-to-skin to prevent heat loss

rationale.correct: First priorities: airway, breathing and warmth.

perOption.a: Drying stimulates breathing and prevents cold stress.
perOption.c: Bathing is delayed until the baby is stable.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize newborn care right after birth.

questions.stem: A parent asks why the newborn needs a vitamin K injection. What is the best response?

options.text: "Newborns have low vitamin K, and the shot prevents serious bleeding."

rationale.correct: Newborn medications: vitamin K IM, erythromycin eye ointment and the hepatitis B vaccine.

perOption.a: Vitamin K prevents vitamin K deficiency bleeding.
perOption.c: That is the hepatitis B vaccine.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 2-hour-old newborn of a mother with diabetes is jittery. What should the nurse check first?

rationale.correct: Newborn hypoglycemia: jitteriness, poor feeding, lethargy; feed and recheck per protocol.

perOption.a: Infants of diabetic mothers are at risk for hypoglycemia.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A newborn's skin looks yellow at 18 hours of age. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Report it, because jaundice in the first 24 hours is pathologic
Document it as normal physiologic jaundice
Put the baby in direct sunlight

rationale.correct: Jaundice in the first 24 hours is pathologic; physiologic jaundice appears on days 2 to 3.

perOption.a: Early jaundice suggests hemolysis, such as ABO or Rh incompatibility.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A newborn is receiving phototherapy. Which action requires correction?

options.text: Covering the baby's eyes with shields
Applying lotion to the baby's skin

rationale.correct: Phototherapy: eye shields, maximum skin exposure (diaper only), no lotions, monitor temperature and fluids.

perOption.a: This protects the eyes.
perOption.b: Lotions can cause burns under the lights.
perOption.c: This exposes all of the skin.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: Which findings in a newborn suggest respiratory distress? Select all that apply.

options.text: Brief pauses in breathing of less than 15 seconds
Blue hands and feet in the first day

rationale.correct: Newborn respiratory distress: flaring, grunting, retractions, tachypnea and central cyanosis.

perOption.a: This is a sign of increased work of breathing.
perOption.c: These show increased work of breathing.
perOption.e: Periodic breathing is normal in newborns.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: Which newborn finding requires follow-up?

options.text: Bluish color of the lips and trunk
Small white bumps on the nose
Blue-gray patches on the lower back

rationale.correct: Normal newborn: acrocyanosis, milia, molding, dermal melanocytosis. Abnormal: central cyanosis.

perOption.a: Central cyanosis indicates hypoxemia.
perOption.d: These are congenital dermal melanocytosis, which is benign.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Tell normal newborn findings from abnormal ones.

questions.stem: Which instruction about umbilical cord care is correct?

options.text: Keep the cord clean and dry and fold the diaper below it
Give tub baths until the cord falls off
Pull the cord off at 1 week

rationale.correct: Cord care: keep it dry, use sponge baths and report redness, odor or discharge.

perOption.a: Dry care promotes separation and prevents infection.
perOption.c: Sponge baths are recommended until it separates.
perOption.d: It falls off on its own in 1 to 3 weeks.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A parent asks about care after a circumcision with a Plastibell. Which statement needs correction?

options.text: "A yellowish crust on the tip is normal."
"I'll pull the plastic ring off after 2 days."

rationale.correct: Circumcision: watch for bleeding and voiding; the yellow exudate is normal; don't remove the Plastibell.

perOption.a: This is correct.
perOption.c: The ring falls off on its own in 5 to 8 days.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A newborn whose mother used opioids has a high-pitched cry, tremors and frantic sucking. Which intervention is most appropriate?

options.text: Swaddle the baby and keep the room quiet and dim
Keep the lights on and play music
Unwrap the baby to cool down

rationale.correct: Neonatal abstinence syndrome: low stimulation, swaddling, small frequent feeds, rooming-in and medication if needed.

perOption.a: Reducing stimulation calms neonatal opioid withdrawal.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Care for a newborn with withdrawal.
